Compressive strength vs. curing time, across five ELA replacement levels
Undergraduate Thesis

Eco-Mechanical Performance of Eucalyptus Leaf Ash-Modified Concrete

Cement production is carbon-intensive, and biomass ash is an underexplored partial replacement — if its effect on strength can be reliably characterized.

Two independent methods, physical testing and finite element simulation, converged on the same optimum replacement ratio.
28.5 MPastrength at 15% ELA, 28 days
0.721 mmlowest deformation, also at 15%

Methodology

Eucalyptus Leaf Ash (ELA) was collected, dried, burned, cooled and sieved into a fine pozzolanic material, then used as a partial cement replacement at 0%, 5%, 10%, 15% and 20% by weight. Concrete cubes at each replacement level were compression-tested at 7, 14, 21 and 28 days of curing. In parallel, a finite element model in ANSYS Workbench simulated total deformation under load for the same replacement levels at 7 and 28 days, giving an independent computational check on the experimental results.

Results

Compressive strength increased with curing time across all mixes, and 15% ELA replacement outperformed the 0% control at every curing age — reaching 28.5 MPa at 28 days versus 24.2 MPa for the control. The ANSYS deformation results independently agree: 15% replacement also produced the lowest maximum total deformation (0.721 mm at 28 days, vs. 0.905 mm for the control). Two independent methods, physical testing and simulation, point to the same optimum replacement level.

All four detection strategies, compared on the same bridge dataset
Independent Research · GitHub

Vibration-Based Structural Health Monitoring

Structural damage lowers a structure's natural vibration frequencies — but so does ordinary temperature drift. The real challenge is telling the two apart.

Each method's failure was diagnosed, not just observed — and the fix was traced back to its exact cause.
24 / 24damage cases detected (best method)
3 / 48false alarms (best method)

Dataset

Real modal-frequency data from the Yonghe cable-stayed bridge (Sarmadi & Daneshvar, 2022, Mendeley Data): 4 modal frequencies identified via Frequency Domain Decomposition, 216 samples across 9 days — 192 healthy (days 1–8) and 24 damaged (day 9).

Why Mahalanobis Distance

Mode 1 and Mode 2 correlate strongly across healthy samples (r = 0.89) because both are driven by the same underlying factor — overall structural stiffness, itself governed by temperature. A per-mode threshold treats each mode independently and misses this; Mahalanobis distance explicitly encodes the relationship, flagging a sample that breaks the normal Mode1–Mode2 pattern even if neither value looks extreme alone.

Methodology & Results: Four Strategies Compared

Fixed-baseline Mahalanobis distance

Mean vector and covariance matrix estimated once from 144 training samples (75% of healthy data). New samples are flagged via a 99% chi-square control limit (df=4).

6/48 false alarms · 24/24 detected — but degrades over time: raw frequencies trend steadily downward across the healthy period (temperature drift), which a single fixed baseline can't distinguish from damage.

Naive rolling-window Mahalanobis distance

Mean/covariance recomputed locally from the 20 samples immediately preceding each point, letting "normal" adapt as conditions change.

7/48 false alarms · only 3/24 detected — the window absorbs damaged readings into its own baseline within 1–2 samples of damage onset, so D² spikes then collapses back to normal and the detector "forgets" anything is wrong.

Clean-buffer rolling Mahalanobis distance

Fixes the contamination problem: the local buffer only updates with samples not already flagged as anomalous.

24/24 detected, contamination solved — but 21/48 false alarms, worse than both previous methods: once falsely flagged, the buffer freezes and goes stale, making subsequent samples look even more anomalous and producing cascades of false alarms.

Linear detrending + fixed Mahalanobis distance

A per-mode linear trend is fitted on training data only and subtracted from the full dataset; the standard fixed-baseline method then runs on the residuals.

Best overall: 3/48 false alarms · 24/24 detected. Fitted slopes are physically interpretable — Modes 1, 2 and 4 show clear negative slopes (temperature-driven softening) while Mode 3 is nearly flat, consistent with Mode 3 having the weakest covariance with the other three modes in the baseline analysis.
MethodFalse alarms (/48)Damage detected (/24)Core weakness
1. Fixed baseline624Vulnerable to environmental drift
2. Naive rolling window73Absorbs sustained damage into baseline
3. Clean-buffer rolling2124Freezes on false alarms → stale-baseline cascades
4. Linear detrend324Only handles linear drift

Independent Research · GitHub

Wave Propagation & Damage-Induced Reflection

The SHM project detects damage statistically. This project asks the physical question underneath: why does damage change frequencies at all?

The same physical principle ultrasonic non-destructive testing relies on — measured directly from a solver built from scratch.
21.8%reflected amplitude
39.2%transmitted amplitude

Methodology

A vibrating 1D medium obeys the wave equation ∂²u/∂t² = c²∂²u/∂x², essentially F=ma generalized to a continuous medium. Solved via finite differences: space discretized into a grid, second derivatives approximated from neighboring values, giving an explicit update formula for each future time step. Stability requires the Courant condition cΔt/h ≤ 1 (used at 0.9, a safety margin below the theoretical limit of 1.0).

Baseline setup: a 1.0 m string with both ends fixed, 100 spatial grid points, wave speed c = 50 m/s, released from a triangular "pluck" at the center.

Core Solver Results

The triangular pluck splits into two half-height pulses traveling in opposite directions, reflects off both fixed ends with sign inversion (expected for fixed-boundary reflection), passes through itself, and reforms as an inverted triangle — matching textbook 1D wave behavior exactly.

Damage Extension: Methodology

A localized region (x = 0.55–0.65, 10% of the string) has its wave speed reduced from 50 to 25 m/s (50% reduction), modelling localized stiffness loss. A narrow Gaussian pulse is launched well clear of this region so its approach can be observed before interaction. Making wave speed spatially variable required re-deriving the Courant condition specifically for this case: the time step must be set using the fastest speed present in the domain, not the slowest — verified by hand that using the damaged region's slower speed would violate stability in the healthy region.

Damage Extension: Results

The pulse travels cleanly through the healthy region, then splits at the damage boundary via impedance mismatch: the reflected component reaches 21.8% of the initial pulse amplitude, the transmitted component reaches 39.2% — both measured directly from the simulation output. The space-time plot shows this clearly: the trajectory's slope changes inside the damaged region (reflecting the reduced wave speed), and the path visibly splits into two distinct trajectories at the boundary. Built at a grid resolution of N=100 (≈10 points inside the damaged region) without pre-emptively scaling up; the resulting wavefield stays visually smooth with no grid-scale artifacts, so no finer grid was needed.

Physics-to-ML Surrogate Modeling for Offshore Wind Monopile Fatigue

Full physics-based fatigue assessment of offshore monopiles is accurate but too slow to run at scale — a bottleneck for rapid site screening or continuous monitoring.

The higher-accuracy model wasn't chosen by default — the decision was justified against the project's actual goal.
R² 0.9936XGBoost vs. physics baseline (log space)
~575×faster inference (reference run)

Methodology

A three-stage physics pipeline generates the training data: (1) synthetic sea-state generation — significant wave height, peak wave period and wind speed sampled from distributions calibrated to published North Sea site statistics; (2) physics-based loading — hydrodynamic loading via the Morison equation under linear wave theory, plus a quasi-static wind thrust contribution, integrated to a mudline bending stress history; (3) fatigue labelling — the stress history is rainflow-counted and run through Miner's rule against a DNV-GL "D" S-N curve to produce a physics-based damage-rate label. This produced 5,000 physics-labelled samples used to train Random Forest and XGBoost regressors predicting damage rate directly from sea-state parameters.

Model Selection

XGBoost was selected as the primary model despite Random Forest achieving marginally better accuracy in this run — both comfortably exceed R²>0.99, so the practical accuracy gap is small, while XGBoost's inference-speed advantage (≈3.52µs vs ≈57.11µs per sample) is roughly an order of magnitude larger. Since the project's goal is a rapid surrogate for screening/scheduling use cases, speed was deliberately weighted more heavily than the last percentage point of accuracy.

ModelR² (log space)MAPEInference time/sample
Random Forest0.99862.8%57.11 µs
XGBoost (selected)0.99364.7%3.52 µs

Results

The physics simulation baseline measured 2.02 ms/sample on the reference machine, giving the XGBoost surrogate roughly 575× faster inference in that run. This figure is explicitly hardware-dependent: across development and testing on different machines, observed speedups ranged from roughly 160× to 660×. Feature importance analysis shows significant wave height (Hs) dominating predictions, consistent with the physics (drag/inertia both scale with wave-driven velocity and acceleration); peak period (Tp) is the second most influential, likely because it's generated as a tight, low-noise function of Hs in the synthetic dataset. Water depth shows zero importance because it was held constant across all samples.
